Amalino: free AAC app for children who don't speak yet
Amalino is a free AAC app for children who don't speak yet: tap a picture, hear the word. In English, Danish, Russian, Ukrainian, Arabic and Spanish.
Words for children who don't speak, or don't speak yet
Amalino is an app for phones and tablets. A child taps pictures, and the device says the words out loud, in the family's own language.

Last year, on a plane, I saw a boy who couldn't speak the way other children did, and I kept thinking about him. The good apps that help children like him are expensive, many work only on iPads, and few speak the languages families use at home. So I'm making Amalino.
Amalino isn't in the app stores yet. I'm testing it on real phones and tablets now, and the first families will try it soon.
Would you like to hear when it's ready? Write to me at {email}.
What makes it different
Words stay in their place

The words a child needs most sit in the same spot every time, so their hand learns the way, just as yours does on a keyboard. Start with a few big buttons and show more as your child grows. Nothing moves.
Your family's languages
English, Danish, Russian, Ukrainian, Arabic and Spanish, with one tap to switch. You can also record words in your own voice, so it sounds like home.
Help for the grown-ups
Children learn to talk with pictures the way they learn to talk with words: by watching us. Amalino shows you where each word is and gives short tips, so you can talk with the pictures too.
Private and offline
No account, no ads, no tracking. Amalino works without the internet, and what your child says stays on your device.
Will it stop my child from learning to talk?

No. Research shows that talking with pictures doesn't hold speech back, and it may even help. It's a bridge to talking, not a replacement. There's no minimum age, and a child doesn't have to be "ready" first.
For Android phones and tablets, and for iPhone and iPad.
Do you speak another language?
Every language in Amalino needs someone who speaks it at home to check the words. If that could be you, have a look.

Why I'm making Amalino
The story behind Amalino: one person making a free AAC app that gives children words in their family's languages. Always free for children and families.
Why I'm making Amalino, a free AAC app for children

On a business trip last year, I saw a boy on the plane who couldn't stand or speak the way other children did, and I kept thinking about him afterwards. I build software and hardware for a living, and I started looking at the apps that help children like him communicate. The good ones are expensive, many work only on iPads, and few speak the languages families actually use at home. So I'm making Amalino: free and offline. If your child uses it, I'd love to hear from you.

Some children have a lot to say and no easy way to say it. Some don't speak yet, some speak only a few words, and some may never speak much at all. An app that speaks for them when they tap pictures can change their day: they can ask for a drink, say no, make a joke, or tell you what hurts.
How I build it

**Research first.** The core words come from studies of what young children really say. About 200 of them cover most of everyday talk, and they keep their place on the screen so a child's hand learns the way.
**Tested by hand.** I try every change on an iPad, an Android tablet and an older Android phone, to make sure it stays quick. Nothing counts as done until it works on a real device.

**Checked by native speakers.** Danish, Russian, Ukrainian, Arabic and Spanish are drafted with the help of AI translation, checked by native speakers. Until a native speaker has checked a language, its text is marked as a draft.
**Private from the start.** No account, no ads, no analytics. The app works offline, and anything that needs the internet asks first.

**Grown-ups learn too.** Children learn to talk with pictures by seeing adults use them. So Amalino shows parents where each word is and gives short, friendly tips, without making anyone feel they're doing it wrong.
Amalino is free for children and families, and it will stay that way. There are no ads in it, now or later.
Thank you

The pictures in Amalino are ARASAAC pictograms. They are the property of the Government of Aragón, were created by Sergio Palao for ARASAAC (arasaac.org), and are shared under a Creative Commons licence (BY-NC-SA). A few pictures come from Mulberry Symbols and OpenMoji. Thank you to everyone who shares their work like this, and to every parent and native speaker who tells me what to fix.

Help translate Amalino
How to help translate Amalino: check a language the app already has, or help add yours. All it takes is a spreadsheet and an e-mail.
Help translate Amalino into your language

A child should be able to talk in the language they hear at home. That's why every word in Amalino is checked by someone who speaks the language, not only by a translation tool. You don't need to be a translator or install anything: a spreadsheet and a little time are enough.
Write to me at {email} and tell me which language you speak.
How it works
Improve a language Amalino already has
Amalino speaks English, Danish, Russian, Ukrainian, Arabic and Spanish. Apart from English, the text is a first draft, and it needs a native speaker.
I send you a review spreadsheet for your language. Each row has the English, the draft in your language and, for words, the picture.
If a row is right, write "yes" in the "OK?" column. If it isn't, write a better word or sentence in the "Correction" column. Leave it empty if you're not sure.
Send the spreadsheet back. I put your corrections into the app and mark the text as checked.

You don't have to do it all at once. The setup screens and the first words matter most, so they come first. Some languages have a few extra questions, for example about word endings for boys and girls.

Do you use GitHub? Then you can also [[fix a translation there]]: every language has its own file, and I check each change before it goes into the app. A simple web form for translators is coming too.
Add your language
If your language isn't in Amalino yet, you can help bring it in.
I send you a translation spreadsheet: the app's English text, with an empty column for your words. The setup screens and a child's first words come first.
Fill in what you can. Even the first page is a real help.
Send it back. I keep your words as a draft for your language.

To be honest, adding a language to the app takes time. It needs a voice that speaks the language well, and a second person to check the words. Your work is kept safe until then, and it will be the start of your language in Amalino.
Until then, families can still make boards in any language by recording each word in their own voice.
On GitHub you can also [[start your language]] by copying the English file. I check everything before it goes into the app.
Thank you. Every word you check helps a child say what they mean.
How Amalino handles your child's data: no account, no ads, no tracking, and everything stays on your device.
Privacy in Amalino: no account and no ads
This is a draft. A lawyer will check it before Amalino is released.
Amalino is made for children, so it keeps as little as possible, and keeps it on your device. Here is what that means, in plain words.
In the app
Amalino works without an account and without the internet.
Everything the app keeps (boards, the words your child used, recordings of family voices, and photos you add) stays on your device, encrypted.
There are no ads, no analytics and no tracking.
Amalino only uses the internet if you turn on an optional feature and agree first:

{app:arasaacFull} and "{app:moreSymbolSets}": pictures come from ARASAAC (arasaac.org) and Global Symbols (globalsymbols.com). Only the word list, the pictures you choose and the words you search for are exchanged; nothing about your child is sent.

{app:naturalVoicesHeading} and the speech recogniser for "{app:aiListen}": the files come from GitHub (github.com), where the voice files are kept. Only the files are downloaded; nothing about your child is sent.
Like any website, the sites above can see your device's internet (IP) address when it connects to them.
{app:syncTitle} and "{app:aiCloud}", which come later: keeping your own devices in sync (end-to-end encrypted) and AI helpers for grown-ups. Each one asks separately, and you can turn it off again.

{app:aiContext} can read the time, your calendar or your location. Each is a separate setting, off at the start, and the data is only used on your device. On Android, the system asks for calendar reading and writing together, but Amalino only reads events. It never adds, changes or deletes them.

{app:suggestHotspots} on a scene analyses the photo on your device. On iPhone and iPad it uses Apple's Vision framework. On Android it uses Google ML Kit: the pictures never leave the device, but ML Kit sends Google anonymous performance and usage metrics about this feature (Google's ML Kit terms; it can't be turned off). It is off until you choose it. If you turn on "{app:aiCloud}", a smaller copy of the photo is sent to that helper first.

{app:offlineTranslation|label} of button words (an AI helper, off at the start) can run on your device. On Android you can download Google's ML Kit translation model for a language once, from Google (about 30 MB, after you agree). After that, translation works offline and no words from the app are sent; ML Kit's anonymous usage metrics apply as above. On iPhone and iPad it uses the languages installed in Apple's Translate settings.
{app:exportBackup} makes a copy protected by a password, and you can delete everything by uninstalling the app.
What Amalino is not
Amalino helps a child communicate. It doesn't diagnose, monitor or treat any condition.
